title: Clear and ambiguous
hook: some verses are clear, the foundation, others open to many meanings (3:7)
carry: some verses are for sitting with

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last verse of al-Baqarah: no soul burdened beyond its capacity. Your line was not beyond what I can bear. Did you read the last two verses before sleep? Day three hundred sixty-three, and a new surah.

A hadith in Sahih Muslim gives the first two long surahs a shared nickname: the two bright ones. Al-Baqarah, which we just finished, and Al 'Imran, the Family of Imran, which starts today. It's two hundred verses long, named for the family of Maryam, and it opens, almost at once, with a verse about reading itself. Before telling a single story, the surah stops to say: not every verse in this book works the same way. Some are meant to be clear. Some are meant to be lived with.
screen: `THE TWO BRIGHT ONES.` → `AL 'IMRAN: 200 VERSES.` → `A VERSE ABOUT READING.`

segments.voice: Here's 3:7 in Pickthall's words. God has revealed the Scripture "wherein are clear revelations - they are the substance of the Book - and others (which are) allegorical." The clear verses are called muhkamat, from muhkam: made firm, tightly built. The root h-k-m also gives hikma, wisdom, and hakim, a judge. The verse calls these firm verses umm al-kitab, literally the mother of the Book: the foundation everything else rests on. The others are mutashabihat, verses that resemble one another, that can be read more than one way. Then the verse describes two kinds of readers. Those with a swerve in their hearts chase the ambiguous verses, looking for trouble and hunting for a hidden meaning. And those firmly rooted in knowledge say: we believe in it, all of it is from our Lord. Now here's a detail scholars have discussed for over a thousand years. The verse says no one knows its interpretation except God, and those firmly rooted in knowledge. Where do you pause? If you stop after God, then only God knows the meaning, and the learned simply trust. If you read straight on, the learned know something of it too. Both readings have been held by respected scholars, and both pauses are known in recitation. Which verses count as ambiguous is discussed too: some name the letters that open certain surahs, some name verses about God's attributes, or the unseen. So the verse doesn't ask you to understand everything. It gives you a floor to stand on, and permission to leave some verses open, without forcing them.
screen: `MUHKAM: MADE FIRM` · `THE MOTHER OF THE BOOK` · `TWO KINDS OF READERS` · `WHERE DO YOU PAUSE?` · then, large: `ALL OF IT IS FROM OUR LORD.`

segments.voice: Think of a verse, or any line from any book, that you don't understand, or that troubles you a little. When the bell starts, bring it to mind and don't argue with it. Hold it the way you'd hold something fragile that isn't yours: loosely, with both hands. Then think of one line you do understand, one that's firm for you, and let that be the ground you sit on. Firm ground underneath, an open question in your hands. The bell holds the time.
Muhkam. Made firm, clear, tightly built. The muhkamat are the clear verses, the mother of the Book, from 3:7. Today's word.

Your line: some verses are for sitting with. Today, when something doesn't make sense right away, a sentence, a person, a situation, try leaving it open for an hour instead of deciding. Day three hundred sixty-three.

screen: `DAY 363 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DON'T LET OUR HEARTS SWERVE.`

howItsDone: Muslim scholars read the Qur'an's clear (muhkam) verses as its foundation and interpret the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses in their light; many ordinary believers simply affirm that all of it is from God and leave hard verses to further study.

fork.setup: you reach a verse you can't make sense of. 3:7 describes two kinds of readers. which one does it praise?
options: the one who hunts for a hidden meaning to win an argument.
the one who says: we believe in it, all of it is from our Lord.
the one who skips it and never comes back.
fork.reveal: those firmly rooted in knowledge say all of it is from our Lord. the verse warns about chasing ambiguous verses to stir up trouble.

original.note: Arabic: the firm, clear verses (3:7); singular muhkam, from the root h-k-m.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Qur'an is either all clear or all mysterious.
what it means: it names its own clear verses as the foundation, and others as open to more than one reading.
what a scholar hears: the waqf question in 3:7, whether to pause after 'God' or read on to 'those firmly rooted in knowledge', a difference held among early authorities and still discussed.
